clinicalPearls: A reactive granulomatous dermatosis presenting as erythematous to violaceous plaques, papules or annular lesions, often on the trunk, flanks, proximal limbs and axillae
The classic but uncommon rope sign describes linear, cord-like indurated bands on the lateral trunk
It is strongly associated with autoimmune and connective tissue disease, particularly rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus
Arthritis or arthralgia frequently accompanies or precedes the skin eruption, giving rise to the term interstitial granulomatous dermatitis with arthritis
A range of drugs, notably certain antihypertensives, lipid-lowering agents and biologic tumour necrosis factor inhibitors, can provoke a very similar interstitial granulomatous drug reaction

Histology shows an interstitial and palisaded histiocytic infiltrate between collagen bundles with piecemeal collagen degeneration and variable neutrophils, overlapping with palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis
The eruption may wax and wane with activity of the underlying systemic disease
Management targets any culprit drug and the associated systemic disorder, using topical or systemic corticosteroids and immunomodulatory agents for symptomatic skin disease
reference.pathophysiology: Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is considered a reactive inflammatory pattern rather than a specific disease. It is thought to reflect immune-complex deposition within small dermal vessels and the interstitium, triggering a histiocytic response to altered dermal collagen. Histiocytes accumulate between collagen bundles and palisade around foci of degenerate collagen, sometimes with admixed neutrophils and nuclear dust. This process is frequently linked to circulating immune complexes in autoimmune connective tissue disease, and an identical pattern can be induced by certain drugs, supporting the concept of a shared reactive mechanism to a range of systemic immunological triggers.
additionalDifferentials: Granuloma annulare, especially the interstitial variant
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing an interstitial and palisaded histiocytic infiltrate with collagen degeneration
Autoimmune serology including antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
Assessment for arthritis and referral for rheumatological evaluation
Detailed medication history to identify a possible drug trigger
Screening investigations for associated systemic disease guided by symptoms
Inflammatory markers to gauge disease activity
redFlags: Newly identified underlying connective tissue disease requiring systemic management
A temporally related culprit drug that should be reviewed and withdrawn
Systemic symptoms suggesting active or progressive autoimmune disease
Atypical features prompting exclusion of infection or malignancy on biopsy
reference.prognosis: The skin lesions often fluctuate with the activity of the associated disease and may resolve when a culprit drug is withdrawn or the underlying disorder is controlled, though the eruption can be persistent or recurrent; the overall outlook is largely determined by the associated systemic condition.
pitfalls: Treating the skin in isolation and failing to investigate for an underlying autoimmune disorder
Overlooking a drug trigger, so that the eruption persists despite topical therapy
Confusing it histologically with granuloma annulare and missing the systemic associations
Not recognising the rope sign as a clue to the diagnosis
